content: Conversion of units involves the application of conversion factors to translate measurements from one unit to another while maintaining the same quantity. For example, converting 6 feet into meters involves multiplying by the factor 0.3048 meters per foot. This process ensures that the resulting unit is in meters, the desired outcome. The method works because the numerator and denominator of the conversion factor represent the same quantity, making the factor equivalent to the number 1. Consequently, multiplying by this factor does not alter the measured quantity, only its unit. When performing unit conversions, the precision of the result cannot exceed that of the original measurement. Therefore, appropriate rounding is typically applied after the conversion process to reflect the correct number of significant figures. Tables of conversion factors are often used to facilitate these calculations. These tables may include categories such as luminance, length, area, volume, angle, solid angle, mass, time, speed or velocity, acceleration, force, pressure or mechanical stress, torque, energy, angular momentum, electric current, electric charge, electromotive force, electrical resistance, inductance, dynamic viscosity, kinematic viscosity, information entropy, temperature, and radioactivity. For mass, it is important to note the distinction between mass and weight. In physics, the pound as a unit of mass is sometimes denoted as lbm to differentiate it from the pound-force (lbf). This notation should not be misinterpreted as the hybrid unit pound meter. Velocity is defined as a combination of speed and direction, with the speed component measured in units of speed. Information entropy is often quantified in shannons, while the storage capacity of digital devices is measured in bits. Uncompressed redundant data typically requires more than one bit of storage per shannon of information entropy. In some contexts, the bit is used as a measure of information entropy and is synonymous with the shannon. Temperature conversions require specific formulas and considerations, as detailed in temperature conversion references. Radioactivity is measured in terms of absorbed dose and equivalent dose, with specific units and conversion factors applicable to these measurements. Modern tools for unit conversion include software and devices. Home and office computers often come with bundled spreadsheet applications that include conversion functions or allow users to create their own formulas. Free online converters are also widely available. Additionally, advanced electronic calculators frequently have built-in unit conversion capabilities. Commercial mathematical, scientific, and technical software applications often include converters as part of their functionality. Popular command-line utilities, such as the Unix program Units, are also used for conversions.
